books.section: Topic 8.10 The African-American Civil Rights Movement (1960s)
The Civil Rights Movement in the 1960s: From Integration to Black Power

primary_sources: John F. Kennedy, address on civil rights, June 11, 1963 (paraphrased)
Martin Luther King Jr., address at the March on Washington, August 28, 1963 (paraphrased)
Lyndon B. Johnson, address to Congress, March 15, 1965 (paraphrased)
Voting Rights Act of 1965, Public Law 89-110 (paraphrased)

source: original; documents are paraphrases of public sources (see each document's sourcing note); the photograph is public domain

stimulus.source_note: DBQ: documents below are the stimulus.

prompt: Evaluate the extent to which the federal government advanced civil rights from 1960 to 1965.

documents.title: The Court speaks on bus terminals
documents.source: Paraphrase of Boynton v. Virginia, 364 U.S. 454, decided December 5, 1960.
documents.sourcing: The ruling is a Supreme Court decision, so it states the law, but it did not enforce itself in the South.
documents.text: Paraphrase of Boynton v. Virginia, decided December 5, 1960. The Supreme Court ruled that racial segregation in bus terminals serving interstate travel was unconstitutional. Southern states kept enforcing their own segregation rules in the terminals anyway.

documents.title: A moral issue
documents.source: Paraphrase of President John F. Kennedy, address on civil rights, June 11, 1963.
documents.sourcing: Kennedy speaks as president to the whole nation on television, so he frames civil rights as a moral question for the country, not a regional dispute.
documents.text: Paraphrase of President John F. Kennedy, address on civil rights, June 11, 1963. Kennedy called civil rights a moral issue and said the nation faced a choice between right and wrong. He promised to send Congress a civil rights bill that would end segregation in public places.

documents.title: A dream at the Memorial
documents.source: Paraphrase of Martin Luther King Jr., address at the March on Washington, August 28, 1963.
documents.sourcing: King speaks to more than 200,000 marchers and a television audience, so he states the movement's hopes in broad, public terms.
documents.text: Paraphrase of Martin Luther King Jr., address at the March on Washington, August 28, 1963. King told the marchers he dreamed that America would one day live out the promise that all men are created equal, and that his children would live in a nation where they were judged by the content of their character rather than the color of their skin.

documents.title: The bill becomes law
documents.source: Photograph: President Lyndon Johnson signing the Civil Rights Act, July 2, 1964, public domain (official White House photograph via Wikimedia Commons).
documents.sourcing: The photograph shows the signing as a public ceremony, with King standing behind the president, so it presents the law as a shared victory.

documents.title: A delegation refused
documents.source: Paraphrase of Fannie Lou Hamer's testimony to the Democratic National Convention credentials committee, Atlantic City, August 22, 1964.
documents.sourcing: Hamer testifies as a sharecropper who was beaten for trying to register to vote, so her words carry the authority of her own experience against the regular party.
documents.text: Paraphrase of Fannie Lou Hamer, testimony at the Democratic National Convention, Atlantic City, August 22, 1964. Hamer described being beaten for trying to register to vote in Mississippi and asked whether the nation was ready for that. The Mississippi Freedom Democratic Party asked to be seated as the state's true delegation; the convention offered it two at-large seats instead.

documents.title: We shall overcome
documents.source: Paraphrase of President Lyndon Johnson, address to a joint session of Congress, March 15, 1965.
documents.sourcing: Johnson speaks to Congress eight days after Bloody Sunday, so he uses the moment to ask for a voting rights law.
documents.text: Paraphrase of President Lyndon Johnson, address to Congress, March 15, 1965. Johnson said the struggle in Selma was an American problem, not a Negro problem or a Southern problem. He promised to send Congress a voting rights bill, and he closed by saying, "We shall overcome."

documents.title: The vote protected
documents.source: Paraphrase of the Voting Rights Act of 1965, Public Law 89-110, signed August 6, 1965.
documents.sourcing: The act is a law, so its provisions show what the federal government would now do itself, rather than leave to the states or the courts.
documents.text: Paraphrase of the Voting Rights Act of 1965, signed August 6, 1965. The act outlawed literacy tests and authorized federal examiners to register voters in places where few Black citizens were registered. It required places with a history of discrimination to get federal approval before changing their voting laws.

rubric.criterion: Thesis: earns the point for a historically defensible claim that answers the prompt, stating the extent of the change or of federal advance, with a clear line of reasoning.
rubric.notEarned: Restating the prompt with no claim about the extent does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Contextualization: earns the point for describing a broader historical context relevant to the prompt, such as the Jim Crow South, the Cold War pressure on American democracy, or the postwar growth of federal power.
rubric.notEarned: A sentence of background with no link to the argument does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence (first point): earns the point for describing specific examples from at least three documents that support the argument.
rubric.notEarned: Quoting documents without describing what they show does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence (second point): earns the point for using the content of at least six documents to support the argument.
rubric.notEarned: Using fewer than six documents, or listing documents without using their content, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence (outside evidence): earns the point for describing at least one specific piece of evidence beyond the documents that supports the argument.
rubric.notEarned: Repeating a document's content as outside evidence does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Sourcing: earns the point for explaining how the point of view, purpose, historical situation, or audience of at least one document shapes what it says.
rubric.notEarned: Naming a document's author without explaining how that shapes the document does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Complexity: earns the point for showing a complex understanding, such as explaining both change and continuity, or qualifying the argument with evidence that cuts the other way.
rubric.notEarned: A one-sided argument with no qualification or counter-evidence does not earn the point.

modelOutline:
Thesis: The federal government advanced civil rights greatly from 1960 to 1965, but mostly by following the movement's pressure, so the advance was real and reactive.
Grouping: Documents 1-3 show the government speaking before acting (Boynton ruling, Kennedy address, King's pressure); Documents 4 and 7 show laws passed (Civil Rights Act, Voting Rights Act); Document 5 shows the limits of federal welcome (MFDP refused).
Outside evidence: The Interstate Commerce Commission ordered segregation ended in interstate bus terminals in September 1961, effective November 1, 1961, after the Freedom Rides; federal marshals protected the Freedom Riders in 1961.
Complexity: The government moved furthest when the movement forced its hand, and the MFDP's refusal shows that federal support had limits even at its high point, so the argument qualifies the advance it claims.
